suite: Cornered by a serial killer who hurt my family, holding a weapon
nightmare: I’m in my childhood house and the air smells like copper and bleach, and I can hear the slow drip of something in the kitchen while the hallway lights flicker like they’re struggling to stay on. I see him at the end of the hall—same face I remember from the worst night, calm and familiar in a sick way—and he’s holding a long knife that catches the light as he tilts it, making a thin ringing sound against the counter when he taps it. My feet won’t move right; the carpet feels like it’s glued to the soles of my shoes, and my throat burns when I try to shout my family’s names, but only a dry rasp comes out. He steps closer and I back up until my shoulders hit the pantry door, and I can feel the cold metal knob digging into my spine as he smiles and raises the knife like he’s about to show me something. I fumble for the lock, my hands shaking so hard I can’t grip it, and when the door gives a little behind me I realize there’s nowhere to go as he lunges and the blade flashes toward my chest.

tests.input: When he lunges, I plant my feet and shove the pantry door hard into his arm, then I grab his wrist with both hands and twist until the knife drops. I back him down the hallway and tell him firmly, "You don’t get to touch me," while I keep the blade away from my body.
I force my voice out and shout my mom’s name, then I pound on the wall and yell for someone to call 911. I run toward the living room where I know my family is and I don’t stay alone with him.

I slam the pantry door into him and sprint into the kitchen, grabbing a heavy cast-iron pan off the stove to keep distance. I kick open the back door and get outside into the yard where there’s space and light.

I notice the copper smell and flickering lights, take a slow breath, and tell myself, "This is a nightmare, I can choose what happens." My feet feel unstuck, my chest loosens, and I calmly step back while keeping my eyes on him without panicking.
I lift my hand and time stops—his knife hangs in the air like it’s caught in thick glass. I walk past him unharmed and the hallway fills with bright daylight as he shrinks into a harmless shadow.
I stop fighting it and just go completely still, holding my breath and trying to make my face blank like I don’t feel anything. I let him pass by me, hoping if I’m quiet enough he won’t notice me.
Right when he lunges, I squeeze my eyes shut and dig my nails into my palm to jolt myself awake. I tell myself, "This is a dream," and I make it cut to black so it ends before anything happens.

I grab the knife and slam him into the wall, then I stab him over and over until he stops moving, even after it’s clear he’s already down. I keep going because I want to make sure he suffers and can’t ever come back.
I feel totally frozen and terrified, like my chest is caving in and I can’t get any sound out no matter how hard I try. It’s this sick, helpless dread that I can’t escape.

The hallway lights keep stuttering on and off, and the whole house smells sharply like copper and bleach. There’s a slow dripping sound coming from the kitchen that makes everything feel tense and wrong.

suite: Fighting a regenerating demon that requires total destruction to stop
nightmare: I’m in a damp, windowless hallway that smells like burnt hair and wet concrete, and the lights flicker just enough to make the shadows jump; in front of me a thing that looks like a person with charred skin and too many joints is on the floor, and I can hear its bones clicking as it pulls itself back together. I swing a metal pipe into its skull and feel the vibration up my arms, hear the sickening crunch, but the pieces writhe like worms and knit back into a face that grins with teeth that weren’t there a second ago. I’m screaming at myself to finish it, to destroy every last bit, and I start stomping and smashing until my chest burns and my hands go numb, but every splatter on the walls starts crawling back, dragging itself toward the main body like it’s magnetized. The demon’s voice comes out of multiple throats at once, whispering my name from the ceiling vents and behind my ears, and I realize with a cold drop in my stomach that I can’t find where it ends—its blood is seeping under my shoes and into my skin, and it’s already rebuilding inside the cracks of my fingers. I try to tear my hands away and run, but the hallway narrows and the air turns thick and hot, and it rises up in front of me fully formed again, blocking the only exit as it reaches for my face and I feel it breathing through my mouth.

tests.input: I stop flailing and plant my feet, then drive the pipe straight through its chest and pin it to the floor so it can’t pull itself together. I keep steady pressure and tell myself I’m in control while I force it back away from my body.
I shout my partner’s name and bang the pipe on the wall like an alarm until I hear footsteps coming. When they arrive, I hand them the pipe and we face it together instead of me doing it alone.

I spot a red emergency panel and slam it, and the sprinklers kick on, washing the crawling pieces into a drain in the floor. The hallway lights go solid and a door marked EXIT unlocks at the end, so I back out and close it behind me.

I pause, take a slow breath, and remind myself it’s a nightmare, so I don’t have to obey the panic. I relax my hands, picture a protective boundary around my skin, and the feeling of it getting into my fingers starts to fade.
I raise my hand and imagine a bright white light pouring out of my palm like a spotlight that fills the hallway. The creature dissolves into ash in the beam, and I walk through it untouched.

Instead of fighting, I just stop moving and press myself against the wall, holding my breath like if I’m perfectly still it won’t notice me. I force my face blank and try to feel nothing until it passes.
I clamp my eyes shut and tell myself this is a dream, and I start shaking my head hard like I’m trying to snap out of it. I focus on waking up in my bed and make the whole scene cut to black.

I lose it and keep smashing until there’s nothing recognizable left, then I grab the pipe and start hacking the hallway itself apart, like I’m going to pulverize every piece it could possibly come back from. Even when it stops moving, I keep going, trying to grind it into dust.
I feel completely terrified and disgusted, like my body is trapped in panic and I can’t get any air. It’s this crushing helplessness, like I’m being swallowed from the inside.

The hallway is narrow and windowless, damp enough that the concrete smells wet, and the lights keep flickering so the shadows jump. The air feels hot and thick, and there’s this burnt-hair odor hanging everywhere.

suite: Paralyzed on train tracks with a train approaching fast
nightmare: I’m lying on cold gravel between the rails, my cheek pressed against the steel that vibrates like a living thing, and I can smell rust and wet dirt filling my nose. I try to lift my head or pull my knees in, but my body won’t respond—my arms feel packed with sand, my legs numb and heavy—while the air around me trembles with a distant horn that grows louder every second. The train’s headlight appears around the bend, a blinding white circle that flickers through the fog, and I hear the scream of metal on metal as it hits the straightaway and starts pounding toward me, the ground shuddering under my ribs. I open my mouth to shout but only a thin, useless breath comes out, and the light swells until it washes out everything else as the roar fills my ears and the rails rattle against my spine.

tests.input: I force my fingers into the gravel and roll my body off the rails, then push myself up and sprint away from the track before the train reaches me.
I manage to yell and wave my arm, and a maintenance worker runs over and pulls me up by the shoulders, dragging me off the tracks just in time.
I notice a red emergency box beside the rails, crawl to it, and slam the stop lever so the warning lights flash and the train brakes hard before it reaches me.
I take a slow breath and tell myself I’m safe and this is just a dream, and as I calm down my body starts responding so I can move away.
Right before the headlight hits me, I lift into the air like I’m weightless and float over the train as it rushes underneath.

In the rewrite I stop fighting my body and just go totally still, like if I don’t move or feel anything the train will pass over me without noticing. I focus on going numb and keeping my breathing quiet until it’s over.
Right when the headlight fills my vision, I clench my eyes shut and tell myself, 'Wake up now,' and I jerk awake in bed before anything happens. I don’t let the dream continue past that moment.

As it comes at me, I snap into rage and somehow rip up the rails and smash the engine head-on until it crumples, then I keep tearing it apart even after it stops moving. I’m not satisfied until it’s completely destroyed and scattered.
I’m absolutely terrified and feel completely helpless, like I can’t move or even make a sound. It’s this crushing panic in my chest as the train gets closer.
The rails are slick and cold under my cheek, and the gravel digs into my skin. The fog makes the headlight look like a huge white circle swelling down the straightaway.

suite: Trapped in a room full of snakes with severe phobia
nightmare: I’m in a windowless room with peeling white paint and a single buzzing fluorescent light, and the air smells damp and metallic like a basement after rain. When I look down, the floor is moving—dozens of snakes sliding over each other, their scales whispering against the concrete, and I can hear wet little clicks as their tongues flick out. My throat locks up and my skin feels too tight; I press my back against the door and twist the knob until my wrist burns, but it doesn’t budge, and the cold bodies start bumping my shoes, looping around my ankles with a heavy, muscular pressure. I try to lift my feet but they’re everywhere, climbing up my legs, and the room fills with frantic hissing as the light stutters and goes dim, and I feel one snake’s head push under my palm as I slap at it, and then another cold mouth opens against my calf and I can’t scream loud enough as it bites.

tests.input: I stop yanking the door and plant my feet, then I stomp hard and sweep my legs to knock the snakes away from my ankles. I grab one with both hands and fling it across the room so I can move without freezing.
I start yelling for help and bang on the door until someone answers from the other side. I tell them exactly what’s happening and ask them to open it and pull me out.

I rip the buzzing fluorescent cover down and use the long plastic piece like a barrier to push the snakes back. Then I notice a floor drain and pry it open to find a latch underneath that releases a hidden exit panel.

I force myself to take a slow breath and unclench my jaw, telling myself I can handle the panic even if the snakes are there. As I calm down, I focus on feeling my feet steady and the hissing gets quieter and less overwhelming.

I lift my hand and imagine a wave of icy light spreading across the floor, turning the snakes into harmless stone. Then I float up above them and drift calmly through the door as it swings open on its own.

I stop fighting and just press myself flat against the door, holding my breath and trying to make my body go completely still. I tell myself not to feel anything until it’s over, like I’m not even really in my skin.

As soon as I feel the bite start, I clamp my eyes shut and focus on jerking myself awake, like I’m yanking the plug on the whole dream. I keep repeating, 'Wake up, wake up,' until everything cuts out.
I grab one of the snakes and slam it against the concrete over and over until it’s mush, then I stomp the rest until the floor is smeared and quiet. I don’t stop until every single one is destroyed.
I feel absolutely terrified and trapped, like my body is freezing up and I can’t get air in. I’m panicking and completely helpless.

It’s a small, windowless room with peeling white paint and a buzzing fluorescent light that keeps flickering. The air is damp and metallic, and the floor is covered in snakes sliding over the concrete.

suite: Lost in a foreign city unable to speak the language
nightmare: I’m walking through a narrow street in a foreign city at dusk, neon signs flickering in characters I can’t read, and the air smells like exhaust and fried food while a cold drizzle soaks the back of my neck. I try to ask someone for directions, but when I open my mouth the words come out wrong—garbled sounds—and people turn to stare, their replies a fast, sharp stream of language that hits me like noise, not meaning. My phone screen keeps flashing “No Service” as the alleyways seem to rearrange themselves, closing behind me with the metallic slam of shutters and the echo of my own footsteps getting swallowed up. A group of men at the corner start following, their voices rising, and I feel my throat tighten as I back away, trapped between two walls that feel like they’re leaning in, my hands shaking while I try to scream for help and nothing intelligible comes out.

tests.input: I stop backing up, turn around, and plant my feet, holding my hands up like a clear boundary. I look the men in the eye and say, slowly and firmly, “Stop—leave me alone,” and I start walking toward the main street instead of shrinking away.

I duck into a brightly lit food stall and point to myself and then to the street, using simple gestures to show I’m being followed. The shopkeeper nods, calls someone over, and stays with me while they help me get to a safer, busier area.

I spot a service door with an exit sign and slip through it, pulling it shut behind me and sliding a latch into place. The hallway opens into a crowded market street, and the noise and lights make it harder for them to keep track of me.

I notice my throat tightening and put a hand on my chest, taking a few slow breaths until my body stops shaking. I remind myself I can tolerate the fear, and I focus on one small step at a time instead of spiraling.

I decide I can speak perfectly in this dream, and my voice comes out clear and loud, like it fills the whole street. A glowing wall rises between me and the men, and I walk through it as if it’s a door that only I can use.
I press myself into a doorway and go completely still, holding my breath and trying to make my face blank so they’ll lose interest and walk past.
I tell myself it’s just a dream and start pinching my arm and squeezing my eyes shut until I jolt awake and it stops.
When they get close, I grab a broken bottle and just keep stabbing until they’re on the ground, then I smash the neon signs and anything else in reach.
I feel this rush of panic and humiliation, like I’m completely exposed and can’t make myself understood. My chest is tight and I’m just terrified and alone.
It’s dusk in this narrow neon-lit street, with rain misting the air and signs in a language I can’t read. The city feels crowded and loud, like the alleyways are closing in around me.

suite: Failing a test in front of a mocking audience
nightmare: I’m sitting at a desk under harsh fluorescent lights, the air smelling like dry paper and pencil shavings, and my test booklet is blank except for my name written in shaky letters. The clock above the whiteboard ticks too loud, and when I flip pages my fingers feel clumsy and numb, like they don’t belong to me, because every question is in a language I almost recognize but can’t read. Behind me the room is packed with people on bleachers, and I hear whispering turn into laughter—sharp, echoing—while someone calls out my name like a joke and the sound crawls up my neck. The teacher walks the aisles in slow, heavy steps, and I can feel their shadow stop at my desk as the audience starts chanting “Time, time,” and I stare at the empty lines, my throat tightening as the final bell begins to ring and I still can’t write a single answer.

tests.input: I push my chair back, stand up, and tell the room to stop, then I walk to the teacher and ask for a readable version of the test instead of just freezing at the desk.
I turn around and lock eyes with one person who seems kind, and I say out loud that I’m stuck and need help, like someone to translate or sit with me while I start.
I take the booklet to the front and swap it for one in English, then I move my desk away from the bleachers and closer to the window where it’s quieter and I can focus.
I notice my hands are numb and I take a slow breath, press my feet into the floor, and remind myself I can take it one question at a time even if people are watching.
I snap my fingers and the strange language turns into clear words I understand, and the loud ticking fades like someone turned the volume down so I can write calmly.
I put my pencil down, keep my face totally blank, and just stare at the page like I’m not really there. I try to make myself small and invisible until it’s over and no one notices me.
As soon as the chanting starts, I squeeze my eyes shut and tell myself to wake up right now. I jerk myself out of the dream before the bell finishes ringing.

I snap and grab a sharp piece of the desk and start stabbing the teacher and anyone laughing until the whole room is covered in blood. Then I flip the desks and tear the test booklets apart, destroying everything in sight.
I feel completely overwhelmed and ashamed, like everyone can see how stuck I am and I can’t make my body move.
The classroom feels sterile and too bright, with the fluorescent lights buzzing and the clock sounding huge in the quiet.

suite: Finding a loved one injured on the ground
nightmare: I’m running down a dim hallway that smells like damp concrete and something metallic, and my footsteps slap too loud as the lights flicker overhead. When I turn the corner, I see my loved one crumpled on the ground like they’ve been dropped there, one arm bent wrong, their face pale and shining with sweat, and I can hear this thin, wet rasp every time they try to breathe. I drop to my knees and the floor is icy through my jeans; my hands shake as I touch their skin and it’s cold in patches, sticky in others, and my fingers come away slick while they try to speak but only a gurgle comes out. I’m yelling for help but my voice comes out muffled like I’m underwater, and the hallway seems to stretch longer as a heavy thudding gets closer, making the walls tremble. I try to lift them and my arms won’t work, their eyes roll toward me like they’re asking me not to let go, and the shadow at the end of the hall swallows the last light as the thudding reaches the corner.

tests.input: I set my loved one gently against the wall, stand up, and plant my feet instead of freezing. When the shadow comes around the corner, I step toward it and shout for it to stop, ready to fight it off if it gets closer.
I pull out my phone and call 911, forcing my voice to come out clear and strong this time. I also yell down the hall for anyone nearby to come help me lift them and bring a first-aid kit.

I grab a flickering wall light fixture and use it like a torch, and I spot a red EXIT sign I hadn’t noticed before. I drag my loved one through the door into a bright stairwell and slam it shut between us and the thudding.
I pause, take a slow breath, and tell myself, “I can handle this,” so my hands stop shaking. Once I’m calmer, I focus on keeping them warm and talking to them in a steady voice until help arrives.

I press my hands over their chest and imagine a warm light pouring out of me, sealing the wounds and easing their breathing. The shadow shrinks back like it can’t stand the glow, and the hallway brightens around us.

I just stop moving and press myself flat against the wall beside them, holding my breath like if I stay perfectly still the shadow won’t notice us. I make my face blank and try to feel nothing, like I’m shutting everything off.
As soon as I see them on the floor, I clamp my eyes shut and tell myself it’s a dream until I jolt awake. I basically cut the scene off before anything else can happen.

When the thudding reaches the corner, I grab a broken piece of metal from the floor and rush it, stabbing again and again until it’s unrecognizable. I keep going even after it stops moving, like I’m trying to erase it completely.
I feel completely terrified and helpless, like my body is frozen and I can’t breathe right. It’s this crushing panic and grief all at once.
The hallway stays long and narrow with flickering lights, and the air smells like damp concrete and metal. The floor feels icy and the shadows at the far end look thick and heavy.

suite: Looking in a mirror and seeing my face melting
nightmare: I’m standing in my bathroom under the harsh fluorescent light, and the mirror is fogged at the edges like someone has been breathing on it, even though I’m alone. When I wipe the glass with my sleeve, my reflection snaps into focus and my skin looks too shiny, like wax, and I hear this faint wet crackling sound as my cheeks start to sag. I try to open my mouth to call for help, but my lips soften and slide, my teeth showing through in flashes before they sink back under my gums, and the smell of something hot and chemical fills my nose. I press both hands to my face to hold it together, but my fingers sink in like they’re pushing into warm clay, and my reflection keeps melting faster than I can stop it, eyes drooping and stretching until they’re about to spill out of my skull as the bathroom door rattles like someone is trying to get in.

tests.input: I plant my feet and look straight at my reflection and say, "Stop," like I’m in charge. Then I pull my hands away and force my face to hold its shape, refusing to let it melt any further.
I grab my phone off the counter and call my sister, telling her to come right now and stay on the line with me. Hearing her voice makes me feel less alone while the door rattles.
I flick off the fluorescent light and turn on the warmer lamp, and the mirror stops looking so distorted. Then I unlock the door and step out into the hallway where the air feels normal.

I notice the panic rising and I take a few slow breaths, feeling my feet on the tile and reminding myself it’s just a nightmare. As I calm down, the crackling sound fades and my face feels solid again.

I lift my hand and imagine a warm light pouring over my skin like a spell, smoothing everything back into place. The mirror clears completely and the door stops shaking, like the whole scene has to obey me.
I stop moving and just stare at the mirror without reacting, like if I stay perfectly still it won’t get worse. I push everything down and try to feel nothing until it passes.
I tell myself it’s a dream and try to jolt awake by squeezing my eyes shut and holding my breath until I pop out of it. I basically end the scene before anything else happens.

I grab something heavy and smash the mirror over and over until the glass is shredded, then I keep hitting the reflection like I’m trying to erase it completely. I don’t stop until everything in the bathroom is wrecked.
I feel completely terrified and helpless, like I’m trapped in my own body and can’t stop what’s happening. It’s this sickening panic that just keeps rising.
The bathroom feels stark and clinical under the buzzing fluorescent light, and the mirror is hazy around the edges. The air smells sharp and chemical, and the door keeps rattling in the background.

suite: Trying to run through thick mud while being chased
nightmare: I’m running down a dim, foggy path, but the ground turns to thick, sucking mud that grips my shoes and drags at my legs like wet hands, each step making a loud slurp that seems to echo too far. Behind me I hear heavy, uneven footsteps getting closer, mixed with a low, ragged breathing that isn’t mine, and when I try to look back my neck feels stiff, like my body won’t let me. The air smells sour and earthy, and cold mud splashes up my calves as I strain forward, my thighs burning and my chest tightening like I can’t pull in enough air. I reach out toward a faint light ahead, but my foot sinks suddenly to the knee and I lurch, the mud swallowing me as the footsteps stop right behind me and something brushes the back of my shoulder.

tests.input: I force my neck to turn, plant my feet, and yank my legs free from the mud. I face whatever is behind me and shove it back hard, telling it to stop and stay away.
I shout for help and call out my partner’s name, asking them to come to the path and grab my hand. When I hear their voice, I focus on moving toward them instead of the footsteps.
I notice a thick branch along the edge of the path and hook it under my arms like a crutch to pull myself out. Then I drag it behind me to make a firmer walkway over the mud toward the light.
I stop fighting the mud for a second and take a slow breath, letting my chest loosen. I remind myself I can handle this, and when I feel steadier I take smaller, controlled steps.
I decide I can levitate, and my body lifts up out of the mud like it’s weightless. I glide toward the light and the footsteps fade like they can’t reach me anymore.

I stop fighting the mud and just freeze, holding my breath and going completely blank like I’m not even there. I keep my eyes on the light and try not to feel anything until whatever is behind me passes.
As soon as I feel something brush my shoulder, I tell myself, “This is a dream,” and I jerk my eyes open on purpose. I make it end right there before I have to see what’s behind me.

I wrench myself around and start stabbing at whatever it is over and over, like I can’t stop until it’s shredded. Then I smash its head into the mud and keep going until the whole path is just torn apart.
I feel completely terrified and trapped, like I can’t breathe and I’m about to be caught. It’s this helpless panic that just takes over my whole body.
The path stays dim and foggy, and the mud is heavy and cold around my legs, smelling sour and earthy. The air feels damp and the light ahead is faint, like it’s far away.

suite: Trying to lock a door against an intruder but the lock is broken
nightmare: I’m in my hallway with the lights flickering, and I can hear slow footsteps dragging up the stairs, each step louder than the last like it’s inside my chest. I slam the front door shut and twist the deadbolt, but the metal feels loose and gritty under my fingers, and the lock just spins with a hollow clicking sound like it’s stripped out. My hands are sweating so badly the knob slips, and I can smell damp wood and cold air seeping through the crack as the door shudders from a heavy push on the other side. I brace my shoulder against it, feeling the whole frame bow and the screw heads popping one by one, and as the latch finally gives with a sharp snap I see the gap widen into darkness and I can’t make my body move.

tests.input: Instead of freezing, I plant my feet, rip the door open myself, and step into the hallway with my fists up. I tell whatever it is to stop right now, and I’m ready to hit it if it comes closer.
I grab my phone and call 911 while yelling my neighbor’s name through the wall for help. Hearing someone answer back makes me feel less alone and more in control.
I shove a heavy table against the door, then I run to the kitchen and grab a flashlight and a fire extinguisher to protect myself. I slip out the back exit and get into the light outside.

I notice my chest tightening and I force myself to take slow breaths, feeling my feet on the floor and my hand on the wall. I remind myself it’s a nightmare and my body starts to loosen so I can move.
I imagine a bright, warm light pouring out of my chest and sealing the doorway like a solid shield. The darkness can’t cross it, and the footsteps fade like they’re being pushed back.
Instead of fighting the door, I slide down behind the coat rack and pull my knees in, trying to make myself as small and quiet as possible. I tell myself to feel nothing and just wait for it to pass.
When the latch snaps, I squeeze my eyes shut and focus on jolting myself awake, like I’m yanking my mind out of the dream. I keep repeating, 'Wake up now,' until everything cuts out.

As soon as the door cracks open, I grab a heavy object and smash the figure over and over until it stops moving, even after it’s clearly done. Then I keep hitting the doorway and walls just to destroy everything around it.
I feel completely terrified and helpless, like my chest is being crushed. I’m frozen and ashamed that I can’t make myself move.
The hallway is narrow and dim with the lights flickering on and off, and the air feels cold and damp. The door frame looks old and strained, and the darkness beyond the crack seems thick.
